name: Illusion of Transparency
description: People overestimate how visible their internal thoughts, feelings, or nervousness are to other people. What feels obvious from the inside often leaks out far less than we think.
design_relevance_note: Useful in creator/social products, onboarding, profile setup, camera or microphone flows, and error-recovery moments: users may feel much more exposed or legible than they actually are, which raises friction and anxiety.
prevalence_note: Widely known in social psychology and communication coaching, and reasonably familiar in creator/social/privacy product discussions, though not a first-line mainstream UX checklist heuristic.

findings.description: Three sets of studies showed that people overestimate how detectable their internal states are to others—including lying, disgust, and nervousness—because they anchor on their own vivid inner experience and under-adjust for observers' limited access.
findings.source_title: The illusion of transparency: Biased assessments of others' ability to read one's emotional states.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky's lying study: overestimating how visible your deception is
applications.description: In a 1998 study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, researchers Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Medvec, and Kenneth Savitsky had Cornell students either lie or tell the truth in front of an audience trying to detect liars. Half of the students who lied believed they had been caught, but only about a quarter actually were identified as lying -- participants strongly overestimated how transparent their deception was to observers.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, peer-reviewed finding about self-perception, not a persuasion or product-design case -- there is no manipulator or manipulated party here, just a mismatch between how transparent people feel and how transparent they actually are to others.
